presentingComplaint: Right upper abdominal ache for ~26 hours with nausea, not settling after antacids
history: 41-year-old man, previously well apart from known gallstones noted incidentally on an ultrasound 2 years ago (never symptomatic before). Since a fatty takeaway dinner the previous evening he has had a steady, dull right-upper-quadrant and epigastric ache that, unlike his usual none-existent symptoms, has NOT resolved after several hours. Mild nausea and one episode of non-bilious vomiting. He has taken paracetamol and an over-the-counter antacid with only slight relief. He is still eating small amounts and passing normal-coloured stool and urine. No true rigors, no drenching sweats, no jaundice noticed, no pruritus, no dark urine, no pale stools, no bowel change, no urinary symptoms. He self-presented early because the pain 'just won't go this time'. Non-smoker, minimal alcohol, no recent travel, no NSAID overuse, no prior biliary interventions.
examination: Comfortable at rest, not toxic, not jaundiced, well perfused. Abdomen soft; localized tenderness and guarding in the right upper quadrant with a positive Murphy sign (inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation). No mass palpable, no rebound elsewhere, bowel sounds present. No hepatomegaly, no shifting dullness, no flank tenderness. Chest clear, calves soft.
imaging: Abdominal ultrasound: multiple mobile gallstones with a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck; gallbladder wall thickened at 4.5 mm with a thin rim of pericholecystic fluid; positive sonographic Murphy sign; common bile duct not dilated (4 mm), no intrahepatic biliary dilatation. Liver, pancreas and kidneys unremarkable.
microbiology: Blood cultures drawn, pending (no rigors, low pre-test probability). Bile not sampled. No prior resistant-organism history.
finalDiagnosis: Acute cholecystitis, Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) Grade I (mild), early presentation with intact liver function and no biliary obstruction
citations: Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) - Diagnostic criteria and severity grading of acute cholecystitis, 2018
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Diseases of the Gallbladder and Bile Ducts
stewardship: Community-acquired Grade I (mild) acute cholecystitis in a low-risk host. WHO AWaRe Access-tier empiric cover is appropriate; a second-generation cephalosporin (cefuroxime) or cefazolin covers the usual Enterobacterales and enterococci sufficiently for mild disease. Anaerobic cover / metronidazole is not required in the absence of biliary-enteric anastomosis or obstruction. Definitive management is early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within the index admission); antibiotics are an adjunct and can often be stopped once the gallbladder is removed. De-escalate/stop per culture results and clinical course.
contraindications: Avoid metronidazole/broad anaerobic and antipseudomonal cover here - no indication in mild community-acquired cholecystitis
Caution with cephalosporins if documented severe (anaphylactic) beta-lactam allergy
Avoid delaying source control (cholecystectomy) by relying on antibiotics alone
edgeCases: Rising bilirubin/ALP or CBD dilatation would signal choledocholithiasis/cholangitis and mandate MRCP/ERCP
Development of high fever, rigors or hypotension would upgrade severity (Grade II/III) and broaden antibiotics
Gallbladder wall gas or non-enhancing wall would suggest gangrenous/emphysematous cholecystitis needing urgent surgery
Elderly or diabetic patients may present with minimal signs despite advanced disease
expectedMaiK: Acute cholecystitis is likely: localized RUQ pain with a positive clinical and sonographic Murphy sign, gallbladder wall thickening (4.5 mm), pericholecystic fluid and a neck-impacted stone, with mild systemic inflammation but preserved liver function and a non-dilated CBD - an early, TG18 Grade I picture rather than biliary colic (which would have settled and lacks inflammatory/sonographic signs) or cholangitis (which requires cholestasis/CBD obstruction).
expectedNextQuestions: Any fever with rigors, or episodes of jaundice/dark urine/pale stools?
How does the pain relate to fatty meals, and is it now constant rather than colicky?
Any prior biliary or abdominal surgery, ERCP, or known bile-duct stones?
Beta-lactam allergy history and current medications?
expectedInvestigations: Consider MRCP if LFTs rise or CBD appears dilated
regressionAssertions: normal bilirubin/ALP and non-dilated CBD exclude cholangitis/choledocholithiasis as primary diagnosis
normal lipase argues against acute pancreatitis
persistent pain with positive sonographic Murphy sign and wall thickening distinguishes acute cholecystitis from simple biliary colic
empiric antibiotics remain Access-tier (cefuroxime/cefazolin) without anaerobic cover
